The Sand shiner (Notropis stramineus) is a small cyprinid native to the sandy-bottomed streams of central North America. Field surveys indicate that newly hatched yolk-sac larvae, which remain endotrophic for the first few days post-hatching, have an extremely modest wet weight at birth of 0.00018 grams [Wwb = 0.00018 grams], a value consistent with the small egg diameter of approximately 0.7 millimeters typical of minnows that broadcast spawn over fine substrates. These lecithotrophic protolarvae absorb their yolk reserves rapidly under the thermal conditions of active summer growth, and the onset of exogenous feeding is marked by the inflation of the swim bladder and the development of a functional mouth gape. Comparative data from adjacent populations suggest that this low birth mass places juvenile sand shiners at an initial size disadvantage relative to congeners that produce fewer, larger eggs, but this strategy is offset by the species' relatively high fecundity.

As the young fish grow through the postflexion larval stage and undergo metamorphosis, they attain a total length at puberty of 3.8 centimeters [Lp = 3.8 centimeters], a size that is typically reached within their first growing season. This measurement is based on the standard length of approximately 3.2 centimeters observed at first spawning in field-caught individuals, indicating that gonadal maturation begins while the fish are still relatively small. The corresponding wet weight at puberty is 0.53 grams [Wwp = 0.53 grams], a value that reflects the accumulation of somatic tissue necessary to support vitellogenesis and spermatogenesis. This modest size at maturity is characteristic of many opportunistic cyprinids that inhabit seasonally variable environments, where early reproduction ensures some level of recruitment even in years when adult mortality is high. Juvenile sand shiners exhibit a rapid growth trajectory during their first summer, allowing them to reach this reproductive size threshold before the onset of winter.

Reproductive output in the sand shiner is strongly influenced by water temperature. Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at 19 °C [T = 19 °C], an individual female can produce approximately 2,600 eggs over the course of a year, a figure that represents the maximum reproductive rate observed for this species. This annual fecundity is achieved through multiple spawning events throughout the summer months, as females are batch spawners that release clutches at intervals that average approximately 1 spawning event every 2 weeks [F_R_i = approximately 1 spawning event every 2 weeks], with each spawning event yielding around 100 eggs [N_R_i = each spawning event yielding around 100 eggs]. At this same temperature of 19 °C [T = 19 °C], the time since birth at puberty is approximately 255 days [tp = approximately 255 days], a value that corresponds to spawning events recorded at roughly 365 days post-hatch when cooler conditions delay development. The synchrony between temperature-mediated metabolic rates and gonadal recrudescence underscores the importance of thermal regime in shaping the reproductive phenology of this species.

Adult sand shiners are relatively short-lived compared to other members of the Notropis genus. The maximum lifespan in the wild is approximately 1,095 days [am = approximately 1,095 days] when the fish are living at a sustained water temperature of 19 °C, a duration that corresponds to about three full g at a temperature of 19 °C [T = 19 °C]rowing seasons. This relatively compressed lifespan is typical of small-bodied cyprinids that experience high rates of predation and environmental stochasticity in their prairie stream habitats. The ultimate total length achieved by the oldest and largest individuals in a population reaches 8.2 centimeters [Li = 8.2 centimeters], a size that is rarely attained given the high mortality rates faced by older age classes. This asymptotic length is considerably larger than the size at puberty, indicating that post-maturation growth continues steadily throughout the animal's life, albeit at a reduced rate as somatic investment gives way to the demands of reproduction.

The maximum adult body mass recorded for sand shiners is 5.9 grams [Wwi = 5.9 grams], a value that is most commonly observed in gravid females during the peak of the spawning season. This ultimate wet weight is consistent with allometric predictions based on the length-weight relationship derived from the species' size at puberty and represents a nearly tenfold increase from the wet weight at puberty of 0.53 grams [Wwp = 0.53 grams] mentioned earlier. Such a pronounced post-maturation size increase is a key feature of the species' life history, allowing females to accommodate larger clutches as they age. The relatively low birth mass of 0.00018 grams [Wwb = 0.00018 grams] underscores the high fecundity required to offset the substantial mortality experienced during the pelagic larval phase, when ichthyoplankton are particularly vulnerable to predation and starvation. Within the genus Notropis, the combination of a light initial mass and high reproductive output positions N. stramineus as a classic opportunist adapted to unpredictable prairie stream environments.
